title: Takata explains his 1.5% vote and the signs that would change his mind
summary: Bank of Japan Policy Board member Hajime Takata proposed raising the policy rate to 1.5% at the October meeting. Speaking to executives in Tokushima on 16 November, he explained why he would move faster after the Board raised the rate to around 1% in June and 1.25% in September. In his assessment, underlying inflation had essentially reached the 2% goal. Waiting another six months could leave policy too loose if firms passed higher costs through to prices for a second time. He advocated bringing the rate closer to the middle of the estimated neutral range so the Board could respond in either direction. The speech records one member’s vote and reasoning. It gives no date for the next increase (pp. 6, 10–14).

The surprise for Takata was how well Japan had absorbed the oil shock from the Middle East. Higher energy import bills usually squeeze Japanese earnings and purchasing power. This time the global build-out of AI infrastructure also lifted demand and export prices for Japanese electronics. The September Tankan still showed strong investment plans. Takata saw firms becoming more willing to raise selling prices, including smaller companies, and thought overseas rate increases had reduced the risk that sharp yen appreciation would bring renewed disinflation. October producer prices rose 7.1% year on year. That figure measures pipeline pressure. Whether it reaches consumers depends on firms’ pricing decisions and the resilience of demand (pp. 1–5, Charts 4–13).

Takata used several measures to judge how much restraint another hike would impose. Inflation compensation derived from inflation-indexed Japanese government bonds had climbed above 2%. It is a traded measure, which can also reflect risk and liquidity premiums. Japan stood out as having low real policy rates when he subtracted observed inflation from nominal rates across countries. Chart 25 places Japan's estimated nominal neutral range at 1.1–2.5%, wide enough to make the response of companies more informative than a point estimate. Chart 26 shows corporate returns on assets above the average interest rate firms paid. Bank lending attitudes, investment, wage setting and price increases would tell him whether that cushion was eroding. A broad retreat in borrowing or investment after cumulative hikes could eventually support a cut. In his assessment, healthy capital buffers and export demand put that point some way off (pp. 10–14, Charts 21–26).

His account of the bond market explains why banks’ lending opportunities matter to Japanese government bond investors. After the bubble burst, firms repaired their balance sheets and borrowed less. Banks could put their excess deposits into government bonds even as public debt rose. Later, the Bank of Japan’s purchases let commercial banks reduce their holdings. Recovery in private loan demand would change the relative attraction of holding bonds again. Assessing yields and financial stability therefore requires tracking which institutions take on duration as central bank buying diminishes, alongside the amount of debt issued (pp. 14–17, Charts 27–29).

Takata also illustrated how household and corporate financing could change transmission. Household financial assets reached ¥2,500tn in June 2026, while cash and deposits fell from 53% of the portfolio in 2022 to 47%. Appreciation of existing assets can move that share without any withdrawals. His illustrations of monthly equity purchases starting at age 22 show how stock-market history could influence different generations’ experiences. They do not measure what households actually bought. On the corporate side, bank loans still accounted for much more financing in Japan than private debt. A larger role for syndicated lending, securities and investment funds could broaden funding for acquisitions while moving some credit risk outside traditional loan books. He presented this as a development to monitor, with implications for how deposit rates, asset prices and exchange rates transmit monetary policy (pp. 17–25, Charts 30–35, 41–44).

questions.question: What would establish that the producer-price shock has spread far enough to justify another increase?
questions.detail: Takata cited the 7.1% October producer-price rise and stronger inflation compensation. Neither identifies the share of services prices rising repeatedly with wages and demand. Compare the next consumer-price component releases, Tankan output-price expectations by firm size, wage settlements and subsequent break-even rates. Persistent domestic price increases across sectors would support his case for moving faster and matter for short Japanese yields.

questions.question: How much does the investment case depend on AI demand and firms still paying yesterday’s borrowing rates?
questions.detail: The September investment plans and gap between return on assets and average interest cost support Takata’s assessment. Aggregate earnings can conceal weak domestic firms, and average funding costs can rise well after new loan rates. Track realised expenditure, electronics export prices and volumes, and interest expense across firm size and debt maturities. A simultaneous narrowing of profit cushions and tightening of lending attitudes would change the policy and credit interpretation.

questions.question: Who is taking the interest-rate risk as households’ asset mix and banks’ lending opportunities change?
questions.detail: The decline in the cash and deposit share could reflect valuation gains, active reallocations, or both. Chart 29 records past bank and central bank bond holdings, without identifying the marginal buyer in the next auction. Compare Flow of Funds transactions with revaluations, deposit balances with loan growth, and government bond holdings and maturities by sector. This would clarify which balance sheets are sensitive to higher long yields.
